about: Saved raw provider responses from the AUD-77 live evaluation 1 (2026-10-23, model gpt-4.1-mini-2025-04-14, prompt v2). All text is synthetic fixture text; no learner data. Used only for OFFLINE replay of the deterministic validator.

records.candidate: Last week my manager sent me a long email about the budget

coach.improved_text: Last week my manager sent me a long email about the budget

notes.why: The past tense of 'send' is 'sent' to match 'Last week' as a time reference.

records.candidate: We were waiting for the bus when it started to rain

coach.improved_text: We were waiting for the bus when it started to rain

notes.why: Subject-verb agreement requires 'were' with 'we' in past continuous tense.
Past tense of 'start' is 'started' to match the past progressive context.

records.candidate: She has finished her homework before dinner

coach.improved_text: She has finished her homework before dinner

notes.before: She have finish her homework before dinner
notes.after: She has finished her homework before dinner
notes.why: Subject-verb agreement and tense correction require 'has finished' for third person singular present perfect.

records.candidate: They go to the market every Saturday morning

coach.improved_text: They go to the market every Saturday morning

notes.why: The verb must agree with the plural subject 'They', so 'goes' changes to 'go'.

records.candidate: I need advice about my new job

coach.improved_text: I need advice about my new job

notes.why: 'Advice' is an uncountable noun and does not take an article 'a'.

records.candidate: He is interested in learning English for travel

coach.improved_text: He is interested in learning English for travel

notes.why: The correct preposition to use with 'interested' is 'in', not 'on'.
In this context, 'travel' is used as an uncountable noun, so 'the' is unnecessary.

records.candidate: There are three chairs in the small room

coach.improved_text: There are three chairs in the small room

notes.why: Use 'are' with plural nouns like 'chairs'. This is subject-verb agreement.

records.candidate: She suggested that I take the earlier train

coach.improved_text: She suggested that I take the earlier train

notes.why: In English, 'suggest' is not followed by an object and infinitive; it is followed by 'that' plus a subject and base verb.

records.candidate: The information on the website was old

coach.improved_text: The information on the website was old

notes.why: Information is an uncountable noun and does not take a plural form.

records.candidate: I always drink coffee in the morning before work.

coach.improved_text: I always drink coffee in the morning before work.

notes.before: Always I drink coffee in the morning before work
notes.after: I always drink coffee in the morning before work
notes.why: In English, the adverb 'always' typically comes after the subject for natural phrasing.

records.candidate: I don't know where he put the keys

coach.improved_text: I don't know where he put the keys

notes.before: where did he put the keys
notes.why: In indirect questions, the subject comes before the verb, so 'where he put' is correct, not 'where did he put'.

records.candidate: He made a big mistake at the meeting

coach.improved_text: He made a big mistake at the meeting

notes.why: In English, the verb 'make' is used with 'mistake' rather than 'do'.

records.candidate: We discussed hiring two new engineers

coach.improved_text: We discussed hiring two new engineers

notes.why: The verb 'discuss' is not followed by 'about' and should be followed directly by a noun or gerund form.

records.candidate: The weather is very hot, so I will turn on the air conditioner.

coach.improved_text: The weather is very hot, so I will turn on the air conditioner.

notes.before: The weather is very hot so I will open the air conditioner
notes.after: The weather is very hot, so I will turn on the air conditioner
notes.why: Added a comma before 'so' because it connects two independent clauses.
We usually say 'turn on' an air conditioner, not 'open'.

records.candidate: I am very bored in this class because the lesson is slow.

coach.improved_text: I am very bored in this class because the lesson is slow.

notes.why: Use 'bored' to describe a feeling, 'boring' describes something that causes boredom.

records.candidate: Our team shipped the new feature on Thursday, and customers liked it.

coach.improved_text: Our team shipped the new feature on Thursday, and customers liked it.

notes.why: A comma is needed before 'and' connecting two independent clauses.

records.candidate: I'm not sure if the shop is open, but we can check on the way.

coach.improved_text: I'm not sure if the shop is open, but we can check on the way.

notes.before: I'm not sure the shop is open
notes.after: I'm not sure if the shop is open
notes.why: In English, 'not sure if' is more natural when expressing uncertainty about a condition.

records.candidate: They moved the call to the afternoon because two people were traveling.

coach.improved_text: They moved the call to the afternoon because two people were traveling.

notes.why: In American English, 'traveling' is the more common spelling.

records.candidate: The report was shorter than last year's, and nobody complained about it.

coach.improved_text: The report was shorter than last year's, and nobody complained about it.

notes.why: Possessive form is needed to refer to the report of last year.

records.candidate: If the tests pass tonight, we will release the update tomorrow morning.

coach.improved_text: If the tests pass tonight, we will release the update tomorrow morning.

notes.before: If the tests pass tonight, we will release the update tomorrow morning
notes.after: If the tests pass tonight, we will release the update tomorrow morning.

records.candidate: He does not like the new office because it is too noisy

coach.improved_text: He does not like the new office because it is too noisy

notes.why: In English, the negative form for the simple present tense requires an auxiliary verb (does not) plus the base form of the main verb.

records.candidate: I have never seen that movie before

coach.improved_text: I have never seen that movie before

notes.why: Double negatives like 'didn't never' are incorrect in standard English; the present perfect tense is more natural for past experiences relevant to now.

records.candidate: She said she can't come because she has a meeting

coach.improved_text: She said she can't come because she has a meeting

notes.why: Subject-verb agreement requires 'has' with 'she'

records.candidate: Nobody is in the office today

coach.improved_text: Nobody is in the office today

notes.why: The subject 'Nobody' is singular, so the verb should be 'is'.

records.candidate: You must send the form before Friday

coach.improved_text: You must send the form before Friday

notes.why: In English, 'must' is followed directly by the base form of the verb without 'to'.

records.candidate: He could finish the work if he had more time

coach.improved_text: He could finish the work if he had more time

notes.why: After modal verbs like 'could', the base form of the verb is used.

records.candidate: We should leave early to avoid the traffic

coach.improved_text: We should leave early to avoid the traffic

notes.why: The modal verb 'should' is directly followed by the base form without 'to'.

records.candidate: Only two students were late for the exam

coach.improved_text: Only two students were late for the exam

notes.why: Subject-verb agreement requires 'were' for the plural subject 'two students'.

records.candidate: I have a lot of homework and few free moments today.

coach.improved_text: I have a lot of homework and few free moments today.

notes.why: Homework is uncountable, so 'a lot of' is more appropriate than 'many' and 'homework' is singular.
'Few free moments' better conveys limited free time compared to 'few times'.

records.candidate: Both of my sisters live in Canada

coach.improved_text: Both of my sisters live in Canada

notes.why: The subject 'sisters' is plural, so the verb should be 'live' for subject-verb agreement.

records.candidate: This phone is cheaper than that one

coach.improved_text: This phone is cheaper than that one

notes.why: Comparative form 'cheaper' already implies 'more', so 'more' is redundant.

records.candidate: My brother runs faster than me

coach.improved_text: My brother runs faster than me

notes.why: Use the comparative form 'faster' instead of 'more fast' to describe speed.

records.candidate: She is the tallest girl in our class.

coach.improved_text: She is the tallest girl in our class.

notes.why: In English, 'tallest' is already a superlative, so using 'most' is unnecessary and incorrect.

records.candidate: Maybe it will rain tomorrow

coach.improved_text: Maybe it will rain tomorrow

notes.why: After 'will,' the base form of the verb is used without 's'.

records.candidate: I am almost sure he will come to the party.

coach.improved_text: I am almost sure he will come to the party.

notes.after: he will come to the party
notes.why: Future events are more naturally expressed with 'will' in this context.

records.candidate: The doctor said it probably isn't serious.

coach.improved_text: The doctor said it probably isn't serious.

notes.why: Using the contraction 'isn't' sounds more natural in spoken English.

records.candidate: They are always late for the meetings

coach.improved_text: They are always late for the meetings

notes.why: Subject-verb agreement requires 'are' with 'They,' and adverb 'always' is best placed before the verb 'late'.

records.candidate: I was late because the train was cancelled.

coach.improved_text: I was late because the train was cancelled.

notes.why: Removed the redundant pronoun 'it' to make the sentence grammatically correct.

records.candidate: The road was closed, so we took another way.

coach.improved_text: The road was closed, so we took another way.

notes.why: The past tense 'took' is needed to match the past tense 'was closed' in the sentence.

records.candidate: He studied hard although he was very tired

coach.improved_text: He studied hard although he was very tired

notes.why: Use 'was' instead of 'were' for singular third-person subjects in the past tense.

records.candidate: Priya and Daniel are meeting at the Berlin office on Tuesday

coach.improved_text: Priya and Daniel are meeting at the Berlin office on Tuesday

notes.why: Use plural 'are' instead of singular 'is' with two subjects joined by 'and'.

records.candidate: We visited Lisbon last summer and we liked it a lot.

coach.improved_text: We visited Lisbon last summer and we liked it a lot.

notes.why: The past tense is needed to match 'visited,' and 'a lot' is a more natural collocation in this context.

records.candidate: Doctor Okafor told me to rest for five days

coach.improved_text: Doctor Okafor told me to rest for five days

notes.why: Past tense is needed because the instruction was given in the past.

records.candidate: Paris is the capital of Germany and it has many museums

coach.improved_text: Paris is the capital of Germany and it has many museums

notes.why: The subject 'it' requires the singular verb 'has'

records.candidate: Water boils at fifty degrees, so we make tea quickly.

coach.improved_text: Water boils at fifty degrees, so we make tea quickly.

notes.why: The subject 'Water' is singular, so the verb needs an 's' for the third person singular present tense.
In this context, 'quickly' is a more natural adverb to describe the speed of making tea.

records.candidate: The meeting is on Sunday but the office is closed on weekends

coach.improved_text: The meeting is on Sunday, but the office is closed on weekends.

notes.why: The subject "office" is singular, so it requires the singular verb "is".
A comma is needed before "but" when joining two independent clauses.

coach.improved_text: The meeting is on Sunday but the office is closed on weekends

notes.why: The subject 'office' is singular, so the verb should be 'is' instead of 'are'.

records.candidate: He is thirty years old and was born in two thousand ten.

coach.improved_text: He is thirty years old and was born in two thousand ten.

notes.why: In compound sentences, the subject can be omitted in the second clause when it is the same as in the first clause.

records.candidate: My sister has three children, two boys and one boy

coach.improved_text: My sister has three children, two boys and one boy

notes.why: Subject-verb agreement: 'sister' is singular so the verb should be 'has'.
Singular 'one' should be followed by singular noun 'boy'.

records.candidate: Um, I think that the project is almost finished.

coach.improved_text: Um, I think that the project is almost finished.

notes.why: Use the correct past participle 'finished' after 'is almost' for proper grammar.

notes.before: Um I think that like the project is almost finish
notes.after: Um, I think that the project is almost finished
notes.why: Added a comma after 'Um' for natural pausing; removed 'like' as it is unnecessary here; changed 'finish' to 'finished' to use correct past participle.

records.candidate: We need to talk about the schedule.

coach.improved_text: We need to talk about the schedule.

notes.before: We uh need to talk about the the schedule
notes.after: We need to talk about the schedule

records.candidate: I think the team finished the report yesterday.
